procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the High Court of Madras dated 13.10.2015 passed in Criminal Revision Case No. 383 of 2015.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The complainant, aggrieved by the trial court's decision to postpone the issue of juvenility, filed a petition under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. The High Court accepted the challenge. Subsequently, the complainant, being aggrieved by the trial court's determination, filed Criminal Revision Case No. 383 of 2015 in the High Court of Madras. The High Court allowed the criminal revision and remitted the matter back to the trial court for fresh consideration.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant challenged the High Court's order dated 13.10.2015 in Criminal Revision Case No. 383 of 2015 before the Supreme Court by way of a special leave petition (SLP(Crl.)No. 1899 of 2013), which was dismissed on 15.02.2013. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal against the High Court's order, set aside the High Court's judgment, and restored the view taken by the trial court.

directions: The Judgment and Order under appeal is set aside.
The view taken by the trial court is restored.
The matter stands disposed of in terms of the directions issued by the trial court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in remitting the matter to the trial court to determine the age of the accused by considering expert medical opinion, when the trial court had already made a finding based on other evidence.

facts: The trial court, relying on documentary evidence as per statutory provisions, determined that the accused's date of birth was 19.10.1991 and that he was a juvenile at the time of the offense.
The complainant challenged this decision in the High Court.
The High Court allowed the complainant's revision petition and sent the case back (remitted) to the trial court.
The High Court's reasoning was that the trial court had failed to consider expert medical opinion to determine the accused's age.
law: The determination of a juvenile's age must be based principally on documentary evidence.
A medical opinion regarding age should only be sought and considered in the absence of such documentary evidence.
application: The Supreme Court observed that the trial court had correctly followed the legal procedure by relying on the available documentary evidence to establish the accused's age.
It noted that the High Court did not find any fault with the trial court's conclusion that was based on these documents.
Since valid documentary evidence was present and had been used, the condition for seeking a medical opinion (i.e., the absence of documents) was not met.
Consequently, the Supreme Court found the High Court's direction to obtain a medical examination to be "completely unwarranted" and its overall approach to be "incorrect and completely misdirected."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, holding that it was incorrect to remit the matter for consideration of medical opinion when the trial court had already made a proper finding based on the legally preferred documentary evidence. The Supreme Court restored the trial court's original order.

issue.issue_text: In a case where an offence is committed on more than one occasion, whether it is sufficient to determine the accused's juvenility based on their age on the date of the last incident.

facts: The accused was charged with committing sexual intercourse on a false promise of marriage on 5-6 occasions.
During cross-examination, the victim stated that the last incident of sexual intercourse occurred in August 2009.
The accused raised a plea of juvenility, claiming he was a minor on that date.
The trial court, based on documentary evidence, found the accused's date of birth to be 19.10.1991.
Based on this date of birth and the date of the last incident, the trial court declared the accused a juvenile.
The High Court overturned this, stating the trial court should have considered it a 'continuing offence' and ascertained the date of the first incident.
law: For an offence that is committed on more than one occasion, it is sufficient to determine the accused's juvenility by considering their age on the date of the last incident.
The determination of age should be based on documentary evidence as contemplated in the statutory provisions.
A medical examination to ascertain age is only warranted if reliable documentary evidence is not available.
application: The Supreme Court found that the trial court was justified in using the date of the last incident, as stated by the victim in her cross-examination, as the relevant date for determining juvenility.
The Court affirmed the trial court's reliance on documentary evidence to establish the accused's date of birth.
The Supreme Court held that the High Court's direction to obtain a medical opinion was 'completely unwarranted' because conclusive documentary evidence of age already existed.
The Court explicitly rejected the High Court's approach, stating it was 'incorrect and completely misdirected' to require an inquiry into the first date of the offence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that in a case involving an offence committed on multiple occasions, it is sufficient to determine the accused's juvenility based on their age on the date of the last alleged incident. The Court restored the trial court's finding that the accused was a juvenile.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in remitting the matter to the trial court to determine the age of the accused by considering expert medical opinion, when the trial court had already made a finding based on other evidence.
appellant_arguments: The determination of a juvenile's age must be based principally on documentary evidence.
Medical opinion should only be used in the absence of such documentary evidence.
The High Court was incorrect to set aside the trial court's finding and remit the matter for fresh consideration based on medical opinion.
respondent_arguments: The trial court's determination of age was incorrect because it failed to consider the expert opinion from a Medical Officer.

arguments.issue_text: In a case where an offence is committed on more than one occasion, whether it is sufficient to determine the accused's juvenility based on their age on the date of the last incident.
appellant_arguments: The trial court's finding on juvenility, which was based on the date of the incident(s) it considered, was correct and should be upheld.
respondent_arguments: The trial court erred by not taking into account that the offence was a 'continuing offence'.
The trial court failed to correctly ascertain the dates of both the first and last occurrences, which was necessary for a proper determination of juvenility.

statutes.act_name: The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000

cases.case_name: Ashwani Kumar Saxena v. State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.principle: For determining the age of a person under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2000 and its rules, there is a clear hierarchy of evidence. Documentary evidence, such as a matriculation certificate, a date of birth certificate from the first school attended, or a birth certificate from a municipal authority, must be considered first. A medical examination to ascertain age can only be conducted in the absence of such documentary evidence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When relevant documentary evidence is available to determine a person's age as contemplated by statutory provisions, a medical examination for age ascertainment is unwarranted.
obiter: To determine if an accused was a juvenile when an offence was committed on more than one occasion, it is sufficient to determine their age on the date of the last incident.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The approach of the High Court in remitting the matter back to the trial court was incorrect and completely misdirected, as it would be an empty formality in the face of a valid finding of fact already rendered by the trial court.
legal_tests_applied: A claim of juvenility is to be decided under Section 7A of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act.
The law on the point of age determination is well settled, as stated in Ashwani Kumar's case, which outlines the statutory provisions for evidence to be considered.
When an offence occurs on more than one occasion, juvenility can be determined based on the accused's age on the date of the last occurrence.
why_respondent_won: The Supreme Court did not accept the respondent's arguments; the appeal was allowed. The reasoning for rejecting the High Court's order (which favored the respondent's position) was that its approach was 'incorrect and completely misdirected.'
The trial court had already made a competent 'finding of fact' regarding the appellant's juvenility after 'considering the relevant material on record.'
The trial court correctly determined the appellant's juvenility by finding his date of birth to be 19.10.1991 and considering it against the date of the last incident in August 2009.
Remanding the matter back for fresh consideration, as the High Court ordered, would be an 'empty formality' given the existing factual determination by the trial court.
policy_considerations: It is an 'empty formality' to remand a matter for fresh consideration when a trial court has already made a competent finding of fact, which suggests a policy favoring judicial efficiency and finality.
